messages.subject: Mapping success and failure (like) proportion phenotypes
parts:
Hi,


I’m attempting to map a  behavioural phenotype in a backcross that takes the form of counts of successes and failures (actually courtships by an individual towards one species of butterfly or another). One way to do this, I guess, is to convert the data to a proportion and arcsin transform it before using scan one in R/qtl etc. 


However, doing this I loose information, and I suspect power, because there is no information about the size of the sample from which the proportion is estimated. To get around this I’ve previously used a glm to analyse these data, something along the lines of:


model <- glm (cbind(num_successes, num_failures) ~ trait, family = binomial)


I believe this in affect does a weighted regression.


With my (genome wide) genotype data I’ve tried running glms for each marker and comparing the associated likelyhood ( logLik (model) ) with the the likelyhood of a null model:


null_model <- glm (cbind(num_successes, num_failures) ~ 1, family = binomial)


My first question is whether: logLik (model) - logLik(null_model) would give me an appropriate LOD score (I’ve then run a permutation test to check for significance of peaks). 


Second, is there a way to do this with interval mapping to account for missing data and gaps between genotypes. Is ‘weights’ (as scanone argument) relevant - assuming I transform the proportions data -  I can’t find much on this.


I thought it might be possible to use the code I’ve written  iterated over genotypes imputated using sim.geno (but I can’t work out how to get these simulated genotypes out) to produce LOD score across the markers and gaps?


That’s a lot of questions. Thanks for any help.


cheers,


Richard Merrill

Hi Richard,

I don't have a specific answer to your question. However, if I underestand
your problem correctly, it sounds very much like the problem that people
are actively working on in the analysis of Chromatin ImmunoPrecipitation
(ChIP) data. See, for example:

Cairns et al (2011). BayesPeak--an R package for analysing ChIP-seq data.
Bioinformatics 27(5): 713–4.
doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btq685

Note that you may also be able to model the counts quite effectively using
a normal distribution after transforming the counts, which would allow you
to directly use the "scanone" function in R/qtl. Again, refer to the work
on analysis of ChIP data for some possible strategies.

Hope this helps,

Peter Carbonetto, Ph.D.
Postdoctoral Fellow
Dept. of Human Genetics
University of Chicago

messages.author: d5fdb09d679f8c32
messages.subject: Re: Mapping success and failure (like) proportion phenotypes
parts:
If you have reasonably dense markers and no selective genotyping, then the simplest solution would be Haley-Knott regression.  That is you regress on the genotype probabilities between marker locations.  Run "calc.genoprob" to calculate genotype probabilities, use "pull.genoprob" to get them out as a matrix, and then use "glm" as in the code snippet you showed.

data(listeria)
listeria <- calc.genoprob(listeria, step=1, stepwidth="max")
pr <- pull.genoprob(listeria, chr=c(5,13), omit.first.prob=TRUE, include.pos.info=TRUE)

You can pull out imputations in the same way using "sim.geno" instead of "calc.genoprob" and "pull.draws" instead of "pull.genoprob".  There is a tricky step afterward of averaging the log-likelihoods from the different imputations.  A trimmed mean is taken, instead of a straight average. This step is explained in the Sen and Churchill (2001) paper.  I can elaborate if you wish.

With regards,
Saunak

Dear Karl,

 

Thanks for your response. I have now done this, but I'm afraid I still have some questions.

 

As suggested, I calculated genotype probabilities and pulled them out:

 

all_data <- jittermap(all_data)

all_data <- calc.genoprob(all_data, step=1,  stepwidth="max")

pr <- pull.genoprob(all_data, omit.first.prob=TRUE)

 

… in addition to my phenotype data:

 

red_court <- pull.pheno(all_data, pheno.col = "court_mp") # ~"success"

white_court <- pull.pheno(all_data, pheno.col = "court_cp") # ~"failure"

 

Looking at each locus in turn, I ran the glm models:

 

model <- glm(cbind(red_court,white_court) ~ locus_genotypes, family = binomial)

null_model <- glm(cbind(red_white,cydno_court) ~ 1, family = binomial)

           

... and calculate the LOD scores for each locus as follows:

           

LOD<-((logLik(model) - logLik(null_model))/log(10))[1]

 

The attached plot compares LOD scores resulting from the binomial glm  (black line) to those from the Haley-Knott regression implemented using scanone in R/qtl. For the Haley-Knott I used the full data-set (blue line) and a reduced data set (red line) which includes individuals with 5 or greater courtship events (i.e. success + failures >= 5, ... so just those individuals with more information). By reducing the data I get a significant QTL with the hk method, but removing a lot of data doesn't seem ideal (if justified). The glm method seems to work (and makes sense in that it should take into account the amount of data collected for each individual), but the LOD score appears elevated. In terms of finding significant QTL, perhaps this isn't a problem as the LOD threshold is also elevated (which I calculated through permutation in the normal way). But, I obviously couldn't apply a 1.5-LOD interval to estimate the position of the QTL. And it looks weird.

 

So I'm not sure what's causing this. Perhaps I haven't calculated the LOD score properly?

 

Could it be that my data are over-dispersed? I would normally deal with this by using quasibinomial errors, but of course it would be hard to obtain a LOD score for these.

 

I'd really appreciate any thoughts you might have.

 

Thanks and best wishes,

 

Richard

parts: Great. Many thanks again.

What you had looks right...the first one.

karl

>
> Many thanks for taking the time to look into this. I really do appreciate it.
>
> Sorry for missing the point but are you saying that, this:
>
> LOD<-((logLik(model) - logLik(null_model))/log(10))[1]
>
> should be correct. In which case I assume there is something wrong with my model (perhaps overdispersion?), or that I should use 2*log lik instead:
>
> LOD<-((2*logLik(out1) - 2*logLik(out0))/log(10))[1]
>
> or perhaps:
>
> LOD<-(2*(logLik(out1) - logLik(out0))/log(10))[1]
>
> ?
>
> Richard
>
>

>
>   # rather ugly code follows

>

>

>

>   logLik(out1)

> karl

> > Yes - sorry I've not been that clear.  That's what I had thought. I had previously calculated the LOD score as:

> > LOD<-((logLik(model) - logLik(null_model))/log(10))[1]
> >
> > But it seems to give inflated LOD scores (by a factor of two as you said previously). I'm trying to find a sensible way to calclate old score for these models.
> >
> > Richard

> >
> >
> > On Tue, Jun 28, 2016 at 8:37 AM, Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:

> >
> > Unlike the non-parametric interval mapping method, with the glm you should have a proper likelihood to work with.

> > karl

> > >

> > > i.e. (in R)
> > >
> > > 2*(model_likelihood  - null_model_likelihood )/(2ln10)
> > >
> > > ?
> > >
> > > 2) Of course I could use the non-parametric approach itself but it seems to give me a highly significant QTL, where as it is 'suggestive' using the normal scanone approach whether I attempt to transform the data or not (I actually can't find a transformation to make the data normal).
> > >
> > > Any thoughts wool be very much appreciated.
> > >
> > > Richard
> > >
> > > ,

> > > My guess is that your LOD scores are off by a factor of 2.
> > >
> > > karl

> > > >
> > > > Dear Karl,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Thanks for your response. I have now done this, but I'm afraid I still have some questions.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > As suggested, I calculated genotype probabilities and pulled them out:
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > all_data <- jittermap(all_data)
> > > >
> > > > all_data <- calc.genoprob(all_data, step=1,  stepwidth="max")
> > > >
> > > > pr <- pull.genoprob(all_data, omit.first.prob=TRUE)
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > … in addition to my phenotype data:

> > > >
> > > >

> > > >
> > > >

> > > >
> > > >
> > > > model <- glm(cbind(red_court,white_court) ~ locus_genotypes, family = binomial)
> > > >

> > > >
> > > >

> > > >
> > > >

> > > >
> > > >

> > > >
> > > >

> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I'd really appreciate any thoughts you might have.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Thanks and best wishes,
> > > >
> > > >
